name: NTEN on adopting AI responsibly in nonprofit marketing
title: NTEN on adopting AI responsibly in nonprofit marketing
answer: NTEN, the Nonprofit Technology Network, published a blog post advising nonprofit marketers on responsible AI adoption. Its most useful point is that AI is not a separate platform to learn but a feature already appearing in tools nonprofits use, from Gmail autocomplete to Grammarly and Meta's ad platform, so the practical task is recognising and governing AI already in the workflow.

sections.body: This is a guidance blog post published by NTEN, the Nonprofit Technology Network, on its website. It is aimed at nonprofit marketers and addresses how to add AI to a marketing toolkit responsibly. The post frames its context around 2023, describing a healing but still volatile economy, political issues, fundraising struggles and difficulty cutting through clutter. It is practical advice rather than original research, and it does not present survey data of its own.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The post's central argument is that AI is not a single platform to learn but a feature increasingly added to platforms nonprofits already use. It points out that using Gmail's autocomplete means you are using AI, and that using Grammarly to improve writing quality means you are using AI. It reports that Meta is baking generative AI features into its self-service ads platform, letting advertisers create multiple ad copy versions for different audiences, generate visual assets and automatically crop images for various formats. It notes that many point solution platforms have taken large language models and added a user interface designed around a specific goal. For nonprofits, it suggests AI can analyse large amounts of data about programmes, audience survey responses or donor details, and forecast trends, and can help with administrative activities such as data entry or creating reports. It gives the example of asking ChatGPT to suggest ways to make a rough recruitment campaign concept bigger, better and more scalable. It advises looking for every opportunity to responsibly use AI-enhanced productivity tools for efficiency, higher quality work output or better meeting goals, while warning that generative AI carries risks including uncertain legal ground regarding plagiarism or intellectual property used.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The text gives no numerical data. Its specific claims are qualitative: that Gmail autocomplete and Grammarly are uses of AI, that Meta is embedding generative AI in its self-service ads platform for ad copy, visual assets and automatic image cropping, and that generative AI carries uncertain legal ground on plagiarism and intellectual property.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For a reader following AI in the nonprofit sector, this source is useful because it reframes adoption as a question of recognising AI already embedded in everyday tools rather than procuring a new system. That framing matters for small nonprofit teams with limited budgets and technical staff, and the Meta advertising example shows how generative features arrive through vendor platforms rather than standalone products. The risk warning on plagiarism and intellectual property also flags the governance question nonprofits face when staff use these features informally.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Nonprofits

sections.body: This is a short opinion and advice piece, not research. It offers no data, no survey findings and no policy guidance, and it does not describe NTEN's own digital maturity research. Its examples are dated to 2023 and centre on marketing rather than the full range of nonprofit operations. It is published by a membership organisation and reflects its perspective.
